title: For Better or for Worse
text:
In the early 1970s, the psychologist E. Mavis Hetherington began a study of families with young children going through divorce, alongside similar families that stayed together. What began as a two-year project in Virginia grew into one of the longest studies of divorce ever done, eventually following around 1,400 families over three decades, including remarriages and stepfamilies.

Hetherington and her team used interviews, questionnaires and direct observation of family life. They saw how hard the first year or two after divorce often was: parents were stressed and less consistent, children were angry or anxious, and many families struggled with money and new routines.

In 2002, with the writer John Kelly, she summed up what the study had found in the book For Better or for Worse: Divorce Reconsidered. Her message cut against both optimistic and pessimistic stereotypes. About a quarter of the young people from divorced families had serious social, emotional or psychological problems, compared with about one in ten from families that stayed together, a real difference. But that meant that roughly three quarters of the children of divorce were doing reasonably well as adults, and many had grown more competent through their experiences.

The outcome depended heavily on what happened after the divorce: conflict between the parents, the quality of parenting, and the support children received.
lesson: Divorce raises risks for children but does not seal their fate. Calm co-parenting and steady, warm care after a separation make the biggest difference.
source: Hetherington, E. M., and Kelly, J. (2002). For Better or for Worse: Divorce Reconsidered. New York: W. W. Norton.
place: The Rotunda, University of Virginia, Charlottesville, USA
